name: Seoul Korean
confidence_why: Jun's production and perception experiments (1993, 1995, 2005), backed independently by de Jong 1994, Kim 2014 and Jeon & Nolan 2017, show that the syllable Lee 1993 calls stressed (the first if heavy, otherwise the second) is simply the high tone at the start of an Accentual Phrase and moves with the phrase, so Seoul Korean has phrasal rather than word stress, though Lee's rule stands in the Handbook of the IPA and Schiering & van der Hulst 2010 still list the question as unsettled. One further first-hand description conflicts (see the conflicting-description item); the entry follows Jun 2005 2005.

catalog_quote: An Accentual Phrase (AP) can have one or more Words and is marked by a tonal pattern, phrase-initial rise and phrase-final rise, i.e., LH-LH or HH-LH. The phrase-initial tone is High or Low depending on the phrase-initial segment: High (H) if tense, aspirated consonants, /s/, or /h/, but Low, otherwise. Typically, an AP does not show any phrase-final lengthening and is not followed by a pause. The four tones marking an AP are associated with certain locations within an AP. The first two tones (HH or LH) are associated with the first two syllables of an AP and the last two tones (LH) are associated with the last two syllables of an AP. When an AP has four or more syllables, all four tones are realized, but when an AP has fewer than four syllables, the second or third tone (H and L), or both, is often not realized, i.e., undershot. ... [Jun & Cha 2015:] Seoul Korean is an intonation langu…
sweep_summary: Korean (kore1280) is coded 'phrasal' on Jun 2005 (UCLA WPP 104 / JKL14). search of 39 title hits (36 distinct works after Glottolog duplicates) plus three on-disk sources. Newly downloaded and read: Kim Kyunghee 2014 Cologne dissertation (KUPS, open), Jeon & Nolan 2017 (Apollo open copy), You 2012, Choi et al. 2020, Yoon et al. 2011, Jun & Lee 1998 ICSLP (actually the contrastive-focus paper), Kortlandt 1993, and Jun's JKL14 paper itself; Jun 1998 Phonology reached only as a truncated the Internet Archive PDF plus the Cambridge preview. Every first-hand source read (Jun 1993 diss. p.35, Jun 1995a poster, Jun 2005 OUP ch. pp.201-202, Kim 2014 pp.35/146, Jeon & Nolan 2017 pp.1,3, You 2012 p.318) confirms the phrasal coding: Seoul Korean has no lexical stress or pitch accent; perceived 'stress' (initial-if-heavy, else second) is the AP-initial rise. The catalog's deciding paper (JKL14) never mentions stress, so the OUP chapter pp.201-202 is proposed as the deciding quotation (same coding, explicit argument). Two contrary statements: H.-B. Lee 1993 JIPA (held by the project; word stress initial-if-heavy else second) and Ko 2013 The Linguistic Review (abstract only, paywalled; word-level metrical head in a two-syllable left-edge window for Chonnam and 'Traditional Seoul', with weak Seoul relics) — Ko 2013 is the one high-priority acquisition. The rest are dialect pitch accent (Kyungsang/Hamkyeng: Ramsey 1978/1991, Kim 1988, Kenstowicz & Sohn 2001, Lee & Davis 2009, Ito 2013, Kubozono 2018, Cho et al. 2019), historical (Vovin 2000, Kwon 2003, Kortlandt 1993), focus/phrasing prosody (Jun 1992, Utsugi & Noma 2006, Lee 2017, Lee & Cho 2020, Kim et al. 2023, Cho et al. 2022, Kim 2004, Jun 1995b), or noise (Yoon 2005, Hetland 2007, Sohn 2010, Kim & Archibald 2024, Jun Jongho 1994). Not located anywhere open: Ramsey 1978, Kim 1988, Kim Soo-Jung 2000, Kim Sahyang 2004, Lee & Davis 2009. OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar could not be reached by automated download; HathiTrust, OATD, MDPI and De Gruyter refused our network; searches were done through Crossref, DNB SRU, archive.org, ISCA/Apollo/KUPS repositories and the Internet Archive.

new_statements.quote: Though researchers agree that Seoul Korean does not have lexical stress, it is controversial whether Korean has fixed stress at the word level or phrasal stress. Some believe that Korean has word level stress and that it is sensitive to syllable weight (H.-B. Lee 1964, 1974; H.-Y. Lee 1990; see Lim 2001 for a review); i.e., a word-initial heavy syllable is stressed, and if the first syllable is not heavy, the second syllable is stressed. [...] Since these f0 peaks correlated with the so-called stressed syllables are due to the Korean intonation pattern, Jun (1995a) concluded that the prominence claimed to be a property of a word does not refer to a word level stress but is linked to a phrasal phenomenon, i.e., a by-product of a phrase level prosody.

new_statements.reading: Seoul Korean has neither lexical stress nor lexical pitch accent. The traditional word-stress rule (initial syllable if heavy, otherwise second) is the AP-initial f0 rise seen in citation forms: Jun's 1995 production and perception experiments showed the 'stressed' syllable carries high f0 and is heard as prominent only when it is AP-initial (occasionally AP-final), so prominence is a phrase-level, edge-marked phenomenon. This is exactly the catalog's 'phrasal' coding; the counter-claims are H.-B. Lee 1993 (JIPA) and, in metrical form, Ko 2013 (two-syllable left-edge window with weak relics in Traditional Seoul, paywalled).

In the Seoul dialect, the tonal pattern of an Accentual Phrase is a final rise, L(H)LH, with the first High optionally appearing when the phrase is longer than four or five syllables. In the Chonnam dialect, the characteristic pattern is an initial rise-fall or fall, either LHL or HHL. [p. 236] ... In fact, the vowel following Coda/A-initial lenis stop is the underlying initial segment of the Accentual Phrase, Thus, it seems that the left edge of the Accentual Phrase is strong in Korean; it shows a lengthening effect [...] there is no lengthening effect at the end of the Accentual Phrase. new_statements.rule_in_words: The paper never uses the word 'stress' and has no section on word-level prominence; the only prominence it describes is phrasal: the Accentual Phrase (a grouping of prosodic words) carries a fixed tonal shape L(H)LH in Seoul (LHL/HHL in Chonnam, chosen by the laryngeal feature of the first segment), and the AP's left edge is 'strong' (initial lengthening, voiceless lenis stops), with no right-edge lengthening at the AP level.
new_statements.exceptions: none about prominence; the paper is about lenis-stop voicing and duration relative to AP position
new_statements.identity_note: Jun 1995 contrasts Seoul (AP tonal pattern L(H)LH) with the Chonnam dialect (LHL or HHL, chosen by the laryngeal feature of the AP-initial segment); three Seoul and three Chonnam speakers were recorded. sources.quote: Stress placement is predictable in Korean. In words of more than one syllable it is initial when the first syllable is a heavy syllable, i.e. one which either contains a long vowel or has a syllable-final consonant because of the presence of an intervocalic consonant sequence. All other words of more than one syllable are accented on the second syllable. An accented syllable is longer and louder than an unaccented one.
sources.note: The word-level view (initial if heavy, else second syllable) that Jun 1995a/2005 re-analyses as the AP-initial rise; the counter-position to the catalog's 'phrasal' coding, stated first-hand by a native phonetician.

sources.quote: In contrast, Korean does not employ lexical stress, fixed stress assignment, or pitch accent in its prominence system. Instead, prominence that may arise with, for example, information or syntactic structure in Korean is typically marked by phrasing or grouping of prosodic constituents, such as a prosodic word, into a larger prosodic unit. In Korean, this prosodic unit is called an Accentual Phrase (Jun, 2014). Such phrasing made by an Accentual Phrase demarcates both edges of a phrase with a particular tonal pattern (e.g., a phrase begins and ends with an LH tone). For this reason, Korean is often referred to as an 'edge-prominence' language, which is different in prosodic typology from a 'head-prominence' language such as English as described above (Jun, 2014).

sources.quote: The location or even the existence of stress in Korean has been controversial. ... I propose that in Chonnam and Traditional Seoul, there is a two-syllable left-edge window, where stress falls on the initial syllable if accented and, otherwise, on the second syllable. Acoustic analyses show that duration, pitch, and intensity all have significant effects in predicting the location of metrical head in Chonnam. In Traditional Seoul, however, only duration and second syllable pitch have such effects. I argue that the weaker relics of metrical prominence in Traditional Seoul reflect the historical shift of its prosodic system from lexical to phrasal.
sources.note: Argues (against Jun's AP theory) for a word-level metrical head in Chonnam and Traditional Seoul: initial syllable if lexically accented (the 'long vowel'), otherwise second syllable, i.e., a two-syllable left-edge window; concedes the Seoul relics are weak and that Seoul has shifted from lexical to phrasal prosody.
